questions.stem:
Statements: All A are B. Some B are C. No C is D. All D are E.

Conclusions: I. Some A are C. II. Some B are not D.
questions.explanation: I: A ⊂ B; some B are C — A and 'some C' may not overlap. NOT TRUE. II: Some B are C; no C are D ⟹ those B (=C) are not D ⟹ some B are not D. TRUE.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem:
Statements: Only a few cars are diesel. All diesel cars need DPF. No DPF lasts forever.

Conclusions: I. Some cars need DPF. II. No car lasts forever.
questions.explanation: I: 'Only a few cars are diesel' = some cars are diesel ⊂ DPF-needing ⟹ some cars need DPF. TRUE. II: 'No DPF lasts forever' tells us about DPFs, not all cars. FALSE.
questions.subject: REASONING

questions.stem: If A < B ≤ C = D, D > E, E ≥ F, which is TRUE?

questions.stem: How did India become self-sufficient in food by the late 1960s?
questions.passage_context: The transformation of Indian agriculture has been one of the most remarkable economic stories of the past 70 years. From food deficits in the 1950s and dependence on PL-480 wheat imports, India became self-sufficient by the late 1960s through the Green Revolution. High-yielding seed varieties, irrigation expansion, and chemical fertilisers raised wheat and rice productivity dramatically. The next phase of the agricultural transformation focused on dairy (Operation Flood) and oil seeds. Today, India is the world's largest producer of milk, the second-largest of vegetables, and a major rice exporter. Yet challenges remain. Soil degradation, groundwater depletion in the Punjab-Haryana belt, fragmented landholdings, and farmer indebtedness all threaten long-term sustainability. Climate change adds further uncertainty. The next agricultural revolution will need to combine productivity with ecological balance — a difficult but essential transition.
questions.explanation: Stated explicitly in the passage.
questions.subject: ENGLISH
